transcript.text: My fridge freezer has been making a funny smell in the kitchen the last couple of days, I've cleaned it out but it's still there. Any ideas?

Yes. Once the inside has been cleaned, the usual remaining source is stagnant water or debris in the condensate drain and its drip tray, often at the lower rear of the appliance. A spill or residue caught in a door seal or drain channel can also keep smelling. 1. Switch it off and unplug it. Keep the doors closed while it is off, and use a torch—do not remove rear covers.
2. Check the floor, underneath edges and the accessible lower rear area for water, a dirty tray, mouldy residue, or something trapped. Any standing water or dirty residue supports a drain/drip-tray cause.
3. Wipe the door seals and the grooves they sit in, as these can hold old food residue even after the shelves and interior have been cleaned. If the smell is burning, hot-plastic or electrical—or the plug, socket or rear area feels hot, looks scorched, or there is smoke—leave it unplugged and arrange an engineer rather than continuing to use it. What does the smell resemble—sour/musty, rotten, or burning/hot plastic? With it unplugged, can you see any water, dirty residue or a trapped object around the floor or accessible lower rear area?
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.

It smells like hot plastic, a sort of electrical burning smell, and it's more at the back of the fridge than inside it. I haven't unplugged it yet. I can't pull it out myself as it's too heavy, so I can't see round the back.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. A hot-plastic/electrical smell coming from the rear is not a food or drain smell; it points to overheating in the electrical or compressor area. Likely possibilities are the compressor start relay/overload, a wiring connection, or the control electronics; an engineer will need to identify the exact failed item. Do not use the fridge-freezer again until a qualified engineer has checked it. Unplug or isolate it now if it is safe to reach the plug, but do not try to move it alone or remove any covers. When it has cooled, you can make one safe check without moving it: inspect the plug and socket from the front for browning, melting, scorching or an unusual hot smell. If any are present, leave it unplugged and arrange an electrician as well as an appliance engineer, as the socket/connection may be involved. If there is smoke, visible scorching, or the smell becomes stronger, keep clear and seek urgent electrical advice.
Ok, I'll unplug it now. The plug feels a bit warm, but the socket looks ok. Is there anything else I should do after that?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
After unplugging it, leave it off and arrange a qualified appliance engineer; it must not be used again until it has been checked. The warm plug makes the plug/lead connection one possibility, although the smell being strongest at the rear also leaves the compressor start relay, internal wiring or control electronics as likely causes. 1. When it has cooled fully, with it still unplugged, inspect the plug pins, plug casing and the visible lead for browning, melting, cracking or a burnt smell. Any of those signs means an electrician should also check the socket and supply connection.
2. Do not move the appliance alone or remove any rear cover. An engineer can safely pull it out, inspect the rear electrical area and identify the overheated component.
3. Keep the doors shut as much as possible while you sort the food; move perishables to another fridge or cool bags if available. Even if the plug and lead look normal, the burning smell means the appliance engineer check is still needed.

candidates: Stagnant water or debris in the condensate drain/drip tray (medium)
Residual spill, food residue or odour source around the door seals or drain (medium)
